hi.label: A
hi.text: In the town of Moynaq, Uzbekistan, rusting fishing boats sit in sand. There is no water for sixty miles. Fifty years ago, Moynaq was a busy port on the Aral Sea, the fourth largest lake in the world.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The Aral Sea was fed by two rivers. In the 1960s, planners decided to redirect those rivers into canals to irrigate cotton fields in the desert. The cotton grew. The sea began to shrink.

hi.label: C
hi.text: At first the change was slow enough to ignore. Then it accelerated. By 2000 the sea had split in two. By 2014 the eastern half had dried completely for the first time in six hundred years. The lake had lost about ninety percent of its water.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The damage went far beyond the shoreline. The exposed seabed was full of salt and pesticide residue from the cotton fields. Wind lifted that dust and dropped it on towns hundreds of miles away. Rates of lung disease and certain cancers climbed. Twenty-four species of fish that lived nowhere else disappeared, and sixty thousand fishing jobs went with them.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The weather changed too. A large lake moderates temperature. Without it, summers in the region grew hotter and winters grew colder.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Not all of it is lost. In 2005 Kazakhstan finished a dam across the northern section. Water levels there rose, the salt level dropped, and fish returned. Boats are working the northern Aral again. The southern half is still desert.

accelerated: Accelerated means sped up. The shrinking happened faster and faster over time.

qs.a: Because the dry seabed was full of salt and pesticide residue, wind lifted that dust and carried it hundreds of miles, and breathing it raised rates of lung disease and some cancers.

hi.label: A
hi.text: In 1952, almost nobody knew what the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean looked like. Ships had taken depth readings along their routes for decades, but the readings sat in notebooks as columns of numbers.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Marie Tharp was a geologist at Columbia University. She was not allowed on the research ships; at the time, women were considered bad luck at sea. So she stayed on shore and turned the numbers into pictures. Line by line, she drew the profile of the sea floor.

hi.label: C
hi.text: What appeared was not a flat plain. It was a mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, longer than the Andes, Rockies, and Himalayas combined. And down the center of that range ran a deep valley.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The valley was the problem. A crack that long suggested the sea floor was splitting apart, which supported the idea that continents move. Most geologists rejected that idea outright. Tharp’s colleague Bruce Heezen called her finding "girl talk" and told her to do it over.

hi.label: E
hi.text: She did it over. The valley was still there. Then an assistant plotted the locations of Atlantic earthquakes on the same map, and the earthquakes fell in a line directly inside Tharp’s valley. Heezen changed his mind.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Their maps, published over the next twenty years, helped convince a generation of scientists that the plates of the Earth move. Tharp’s name did not appear on the first paper announcing the discovery.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Venice, Italy is built on 118 small islands in a lagoon. Its buildings do not rest on rock. They rest on millions of wooden posts driven down into mud, a technique that has held for more than a thousand years.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The city is sinking and the water is rising, and those two problems have completely different causes.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The sinking has two sources. Some of it is natural: the soft ground compacts slowly under the weight of the city. The rest was self-inflicted. In the middle of the twentieth century, factories on the mainland pumped groundwater out from under the lagoon, and the ground above the emptied space settled. Venice dropped about twelve centimeters before the pumping was banned in the 1970s.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The rising is global. Warmer oceans expand, and melting ice adds volume. Sea level in the northern Adriatic has climbed roughly thirty centimeters over the last century.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Combined, the two effects flood St. Mark’s Square more than sixty times a year. A century ago it flooded fewer than ten.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Venice’s answer is a set of 78 steel gates that lie flat on the sea floor at the three entrances to the lagoon. When a high tide is forecast, compressed air pushes the water out of the gates and they swing up into a wall. The system first protected the city in 2020. It cost more than five billion euros and took eighteen years to finish.

qs.a: Factories on the mainland pumped groundwater out from under the lagoon, and the ground settled into the emptied space, dropping the city about twelve centimeters.

qs.a: Because factories pumped water out from under the lagoon, the space that water had filled collapsed, the ground above settled, and the whole city dropped about twelve centimeters.

hi.label: A
hi.text: On October 30, 1938, the Mercury Theatre broadcast a radio play based on H.G. Wells’s novel The War of the Worlds. The script was written as a series of news bulletins interrupting a program of dance music.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The format mattered. Listeners heard what sounded like a real reporter describing a cylinder opening in a New Jersey field, then a heat ray, then the broadcast itself collapsing into static. An announcer stated at the opening that the program was fiction, but many people tuned in late.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Newspapers the next morning described mass panic: crowds in the streets, jammed switchboards, families fleeing cities. The story became famous, and it is still repeated in classrooms today.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Later researchers questioned it. Ratings data showed that relatively few people were listening, because a popular comedy program held most of the audience in that hour. Surveys taken afterward found that most listeners who did hear the show understood it was a play.

hi.label: E
hi.text: So why did the panic story spread? Newspapers at the time were losing advertising money to radio. A story about radio being reckless and dangerous served their interests. Historians now believe the papers inflated a small number of frightened phone calls into a national event.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The broadcast is still a useful lesson, though perhaps not the one usually taught. The audience was not as gullible as the story claims. The people who repeated the story were.

lo.label: A
lo.text: On October 30, 1938, a radio show told a story about aliens invading Earth. The script was written to sound like news bulletins breaking into a music program.

lo.label: B
lo.text: That choice mattered. Listeners heard what sounded like a real reporter describing a cylinder opening in a New Jersey field. An announcer said at the start that it was fiction, but many people tuned in late.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The next morning, newspapers said people had panicked. They wrote about crowds in the streets and jammed phone lines. That story is still repeated today.

lo.label: D
lo.text: Later researchers doubted it. Ratings showed few people were listening. Surveys found that most who did hear it knew it was a play.

lo.label: E
lo.text: So why did the panic story spread? Newspapers were losing money to radio. A story about radio being dangerous helped them. Historians think the papers turned a few scared phone calls into a national panic.

lo.label: F
lo.text: The broadcast still teaches a lesson, but maybe not the usual one. The listeners were not as easily fooled as the story says. The people repeating the story were.

qs.q: What evidence made later researchers doubt the panic story?
qs.a: Ratings data showed relatively few people were listening because a popular comedy held most of the audience, and surveys afterward found most listeners who did hear the show knew it was a play.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. format) and paragraph E (i.e. motive).
Summarize why the story of the 1938 panic may not be accurate.
qs.a: The broadcast was written as fake news bulletins, and newspapers reported the next day that listeners had panicked. But ratings showed few people were listening and surveys showed most knew it was fiction. Newspapers were losing money to radio and had a reason to exaggerate, so historians think the panic was largely invented.

qs.q:
bulletins: Bulletins are short news reports that interrupt regular programming to announce something urgent.
gullible: Gullible means easily fooled, or quick to believe something without checking it.
Describe the connection between newspaper advertising money and the panic story.
qs.a: Because newspapers were losing advertising money to radio, a story showing radio as reckless served their interests, so they had a reason to inflate a few frightened calls into a national panic.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you see rings. Each ring is one year of growth: a pale band of fast spring growth and a dark band of slow summer growth. Counting them gives the tree’s age. Measuring them gives much more.

hi.label: B
hi.text: A wide ring means a good year with plenty of water. A narrow ring means drought. Because every tree in a region lives through the same weather, trees of the same species in the same place share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a little like a barcode.

hi.label: C
hi.text: That shared pattern is what makes the method powerful. A scientist can overlap the rings of a living tree with the outer rings of an older dead log, then overlap that log with an even older beam, and keep stepping backward. In the American Southwest, this chain of overlaps reaches back more than two thousand years.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Archaeologists use it to date buildings. A wooden beam in a cliff dwelling can be matched to the master pattern, which gives the exact year that tree was cut. That is how we know the largest structures at Chaco Canyon went up in bursts of building rather than steadily.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Climate scientists use it differently. The rings preserve a record of rainfall from long before anyone was measuring rainfall. Tree rings show that a drought in the Southwest in the late 1200s lasted more than twenty years, which matches the period when many cliff dwellings were abandoned.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The tree does not know it is keeping records. It simply grows more in a wet year than a dry one. Everything else is us learning to read.

lo.label: B

lo.label: C
lo.text: That shared pattern is the key. A scientist can match the rings of a living tree to an older dead log, then match that log to an even older beam, and keep stepping back. In the Southwest, the chain reaches back more than two thousand years.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Climate scientists use it another way. The rings record rainfall from before anyone measured rainfall. They show a drought in the late 1200s that lasted more than twenty years. That is when many cliff dwellings were left empty.

lo.label: F
lo.text: The tree does not know it is keeping records. It just grows more in a wet year. The reading is up to us.

qs.q: Why can scientists date wood that is far older than any living tree?
qs.a: Because trees in one region share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a scientist can overlap a living tree with an older dead log, then that log with an even older beam, stepping backward thousands of years.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. pattern) and paragraph E (i.e. climate).
Summarize what tree rings can tell us and how scientists read them.
qs.a: Each ring is one year, and its width shows how wet that year was. Trees in one region share the same pattern, so scientists overlap living trees with older and older wood to build a chain going back thousands of years. Archaeologists use it to date buildings to the exact year, and climate scientists use it to find droughts that happened before rainfall was ever measured.

qs.q:
drought: A drought is a long stretch of time with much less rain than normal.
archaeologists: Archaeologists are scientists who study people of the past by examining what they built and left behind.
Describe the connection between the drought of the late 1200s and the cliff dwellings.
qs.a: Because tree rings show a drought lasting more than twenty years in the late 1200s, and that is the same period when many cliff dwellings were abandoned, the drought is a likely reason people left.

hi.label: A
hi.text: For centuries, a ship at sea could tell how far north or south it was by measuring the sun. Nobody could reliably tell how far east or west. Ships missed islands by hundreds of miles. Crews starved. In 1707, four British warships ran into rocks off England and about fourteen hundred men died.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The math was not the hard part. The Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. If a sailor knew the exact time at home and the exact time where the ship was, the difference would give the longitude. The problem was knowing the time back home.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Clocks of the day used a swinging pendulum. On a rolling ship a pendulum is useless. Heat, cold, and salt air threw the mechanism off further. Britain offered a prize worth millions in today’s money to anyone who could solve it.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Most experts worked on maps of the moon and stars. A carpenter named John Harrison built a clock instead. He replaced the pendulum with springs that balanced each other, so rocking did not matter. He used two metals that expanded at different rates, so the clock corrected itself as the temperature changed.

hi.label: E
hi.text: His fourth version was the size of a large pocket watch. On a voyage to Jamaica in 1761 it lost about five seconds in eighty-one days.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The board that judged the prize was full of astronomers, and they kept demanding new trials. Harrison spent forty years on the clocks and most of his life arguing for the money. He was finally paid at the age of eighty.

qs.q: Why could sailors find their latitude but not their longitude?

qs.a: Ships could not tell how far east or west they were, and wrecks killed thousands. qs.q:

trials: Trials are tests done to prove whether something works.
Describe the connection between the two metals in the clock and its accuracy.
qs.a: Because the two metals expanded at different rates, they pulled against each other as the temperature changed, which corrected the mechanism and kept the clock running at the same speed in heat and cold.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Rivers do not stay where we put them. Over thousands of years the Mississippi has swung back and forth across southern Louisiana, building land in one place and abandoning it for another. Roughly every thousand years it finds a shorter path to the sea and takes it.

hi.label: B
hi.text: By the 1950s it had found one. A smaller river called the Atchafalaya offered a route to the Gulf less than half as long as the Mississippi’s own. Water flows toward the steeper, shorter path. Each year a little more of the Mississippi went that way.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The consequences would have been enormous. Baton Rouge and New Orleans sit on the Mississippi. So do oil refineries, chemical plants, and the port that handles much of the country’s grain. If the river left, their water would turn salty and their shipping channel would become a shallow bay.

hi.label: D
hi.text: So the Army Corps of Engineers built the Old River Control Structure: a set of concrete gates that lets exactly thirty percent of the flow into the Atchafalaya and holds the rest in the Mississippi. It opened in 1963.

hi.label: E
hi.text: In 1973 a flood nearly ended it. Water scoured a hole under one of the structures deep enough to swallow a building. Engineers dropped boulders in for weeks. The structure held, but a wing of it collapsed, and afterward the Corps built a second structure beside the first as backup.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The river has not stopped trying. Every year the gates hold a continent’s worth of water on a path it no longer wants to take.

hi.label: A
hi.text: On a frozen island between Norway and the North Pole, a concrete wedge sticks out of a mountainside. A tunnel runs four hundred feet into the rock. At the end are three rooms holding seeds.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a backup copy of the world’s crops. Countries send duplicate samples of their seeds, sealed in foil packets and boxed. It holds more than a million varieties: thousands of kinds of rice, wheat, beans, and potatoes that most people have never heard of.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Variety is the point. A crop grown from one single variety can be wiped out by one disease. When a blight destroyed Ireland’s potatoes in the 1840s, nearly all of them were the same kind. Old and rare varieties carry traits, like resistance to a fungus or tolerance for salty soil, that plant breeders may need later.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The location was chosen for physics, not scenery. The rock stays below freezing on its own, so even if the power failed the seeds would stay cold for weeks. The vault sits well above sea level.

hi.label: E
hi.text: It has been used once. The seed bank in Aleppo, Syria was damaged in the civil war, and researchers withdrew samples from Svalbard to restart their collection in Lebanon and Morocco. They later sent replacements back.

hi.label: F

hi.label: A
hi.text: In January 1814 Londoners walked out onto the middle of the River Thames, set up tents, and held a fair. There were swings, printing presses selling souvenirs, and an elephant led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge.

hi.label: B
hi.text: These frost fairs happened more than once. The river froze solid enough to hold crowds at least two dozen times between the 1300s and 1814. Two conditions had to line up.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The first was climate. Europe was passing through a stretch of unusually cold centuries now called the Little Ice Age. Winters ran longer and harder than they do today.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The second was the river itself. Old London Bridge sat on nineteen wide stone piers, and those piers left only narrow gaps for water to pass. The bridge acted like a dam. Upstream the current slowed almost to nothing, and slow shallow water freezes far more easily than fast deep water.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The 1814 fair was the last one. In 1831 the old bridge was replaced with a new one on fewer, wider arches, and the river ran faster. Embankments built later narrowed and deepened the channel, speeding it further.

hi.label: F
hi.text: So the fairs did not end only because the climate warmed. They ended because people rebuilt the river. Even in the coldest winters since, the Thames through London has not frozen across.

hi.text: Your immune system is good at fighting an enemy it has already met. The first time a germ arrives, it takes about a week to build the right defense, and you are sick for that week. The second time, the defense is ready in hours and you may never notice.

hi.label: B
hi.text: A vaccine is a way of getting the practice without the illness.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Your immune cells find the piece and treat it as an intruder. They build antibodies shaped to lock onto it, the way a key fits one lock. Then, and this is the important part, some of those cells become memory cells and stay in your body for years.

hi.label: E
hi.text: If the real germ ever arrives, the memory cells recognize the shape immediately and the antibodies are produced fast enough to stop the infection before it spreads.

hi.label: F

hi.label: A
hi.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in Washington State in July 1940 and collapsed four months later. Film of the collapse is still shown in engineering classes, because the bridge did not fall the way anyone expected.

hi.label: B
hi.text: It was built long, narrow, and unusually light. Instead of an open truss under the roadway, the designers used solid steel plate girders eight feet deep along the sides. Those plates were the problem: wind could not pass through them, so it had to go around.

hi.label: C
hi.text: From the first days, the deck rippled up and down in ordinary wind. Drivers came for the ride. Locals called the bridge Galloping Gertie. Engineers attached cables and hydraulic devices to damp the motion, and the rippling continued.

hi.label: D
hi.text: On November 7, 1940, a steady wind near forty miles an hour did something different. The deck stopped rippling and began to twist, one edge rising as the other fell. Wind curling off the solid girders shed swirls of air in a rhythm, and that rhythm matched the bridge’s own natural twisting motion. Each gust arrived at the moment that pushed the twist further, the way timing your legs makes a swing go higher.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The twisting grew for about an hour until the deck tore loose and fell into the water. Nobody died. A dog left in an abandoned car did not survive.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Bridges built since are tested as models in wind tunnels, and most use open trusses or shaped decks that let wind slip past instead of catching it.

hi.text: In the middle of the Sahara, on rock walls in southern Algeria and Libya, there are paintings of people swimming. There are herds of cattle, hippos, crocodiles, and giraffes. The nearest permanent water today is hundreds of miles away.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The paintings are not imaginary. Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago the Sahara was grassland dotted with lakes. Lake Chad covered an area larger than the Caspian Sea. Rivers ran where there is now nothing but sand.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The cause was the tilt and wobble of the Earth. Our planet’s axis shifts slowly over tens of thousands of years, changing how much summer sunlight reaches each latitude. During that period, North Africa received more summer sun. Hotter land pulled moist air inland from the ocean, and the monsoon rains that now stop far to the south reached deep into the desert.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Vegetation made it stronger. Plants hold moisture and release it back into the air, and dark leaves absorb more heat than pale sand does. Green ground pulls in more rain, which grows more green ground.

hi.label: E
hi.text: That same loop ran in reverse when the sunlight faded. Less rain killed plants, bare sand reflected sunlight back into space, the land cooled, and the rain retreated further. The change was not gradual everywhere; in some places the record suggests it took only a few centuries.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The wobble continues. On the current cycle, the monsoon is expected to reach into the Sahara again in roughly 15,000 years.

lo.text: In the middle of the Sahara there are rock paintings of people swimming. There are cattle, hippos, and giraffes. The nearest water today is hundreds of miles away.

lo.label: F

qs.a: The slow shift in Earth’s tilt gave North Africa more summer sunlight. The hotter land pulled moist ocean air inland, so monsoon rains that now stop far to the south reached deep into the desert.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Ships do not drive through the locks under their own power. Small electric locomotives called mules run on tracks along the walls, holding the ship centered with cables. The clearance in the older locks is about two feet on each side.

Summarize how a ship gets from one ocean to the other through the canal.
qs.a: A ship enters a lock chamber and the gate closes. Valves let higher water flow in by gravity until the ship has floated up to the next level, and the upper gate opens. The ship crosses the lake eighty-five feet up, then descends the same way as valves drain each chamber. Electric mules keep it centered.

qs.q:
valves: Valves are controls that open and close to let water flow through a pipe or tunnel.
clearance: Clearance is the space left between two things, here between the ship and the lock wall.
Describe the connection between rainfall and how many ships can use the canal.
qs.a: Because every lift dumps about 26 million gallons into the ocean and none of it is recovered, the canal depends on rain refilling Gatun Lake, so a drought forces it to run fewer ships.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Before refrigeration, salt was not a seasoning. It was the only reliable way to keep food from rotting, and that made it valuable enough to fight wars over.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Salt preserves meat by pulling water out of it. Bacteria need moisture to multiply, so a salted ham is a place where bacteria cannot get started. A cut of pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Because it was essential and hard to get, salt became a commodity, a good traded in bulk at a set price. Roman soldiers received an allowance to buy it, and the Latin word for that payment, salarium, is where the English word salary comes from.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Governments noticed. A tax on salt is difficult to avoid, because everyone needs it and there is no substitute. France collected the gabelle, a salt tax so resented it helped fuel a revolution. In India, British law made it illegal to collect salt from the sea, and in 1930 Gandhi walked 240 miles to the coast to break that law in public.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Refrigeration ended salt’s monopoly in about fifty years. Today it is one of the cheapest minerals on Earth, spread on roads by the ton.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Its value never came from the substance. It came from scarcity, and from the fact that nothing else would do.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Before refrigerators, salt was not just a seasoning. It was the only sure way to keep food from rotting. That made it worth fighting over.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Salt keeps meat by pulling water out of it. Bacteria need water to grow, so they cannot get started in salted meat. Pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Because everyone needed it, salt became a commodity, a good traded in bulk at a set price. Roman soldiers were given money to buy it. The Latin word for that payment is where we get the word salary.

lo.label: D

lo.label: E
lo.text: Refrigeration ended all of it in about fifty years. Today salt is one of the cheapest minerals on Earth.

qs.q: Explain how salt preserves meat.
qs.a: Salt pulls the water out of meat. Bacteria need moisture to multiply, so without it they cannot get started, and pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. trade) and paragraph D (i.e. taxes).
Summarize why salt was once so valuable and why it is not now.
qs.a: Salt was the only reliable way to keep food from spoiling, and because it was essential and hard to get, it was traded as a commodity, paid to soldiers, and taxed by governments. Refrigeration gave people another way to preserve food, so salt lost its scarcity and became cheap.

qs.q:
commodity: A commodity is a basic good traded in large amounts at a set price, like salt, grain, or oil.
scarcity: Scarcity is a short supply of something people need. Salt was valuable because of scarcity, not because of what it was.
Describe the connection between a good having no substitute and a government taxing it.
qs.a: Because everyone needs salt and nothing else will do the job, people cannot avoid buying it, so a tax on salt collects money from nearly every household.

hi.label: A
hi.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mold growing on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. That accident became penicillin, and infections that routinely killed people became treatable within twenty years.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Fleming warned about the problem himself. Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes, and each generation carries small random mutations. In any large population, a few bacteria happen to carry a mutation that lets them survive a given drug.

hi.label: C
hi.text: That is where selection takes over. When the antibiotic kills the vulnerable bacteria, the resistant few are left with no competition and multiply freely. The drug did not create the resistance. It cleared the field for it.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Two habits speed this up. Taking antibiotics for a viral illness like a cold does nothing to the virus but exposes the bacteria in your body to the drug for no reason. Stopping a prescription early because you feel better leaves the hardiest bacteria alive to rebuild.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Some infections are now resistant to nearly every drug available. Developing a new antibiotic takes about a decade, and resistance to it can appear within a few years.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The strategy now is to slow the process down: use the drugs only when they will work, finish the course, and hold the strongest ones in reserve.

lo.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mold on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. That accident became penicillin.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Fleming warned about the problem himself. Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes, and each new generation has small random changes. A few happen to survive a given drug.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Then selection takes over. The drug kills the weak bacteria, and the resistant few are left with no competition. The drug did not create the resistance. It cleared the field for it.

lo.label: D

lo.label: E
lo.text: Some infections now resist nearly every drug. A new antibiotic takes about ten years to develop, and resistance can appear within a few years.

qs.q: Explain why the author says the drug did not create the resistance.
qs.a: The resistant bacteria were already there, carrying random mutations. The antibiotic killed the vulnerable ones, which left the resistant few with no competition and room to multiply.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. selection) and paragraph D (i.e. habits).
Summarize how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
qs.a: Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes with small random mutations, so a few in any population survive a given drug. When the antibiotic kills the rest, those survivors multiply without competition. Using antibiotics on viruses or stopping a course early speeds the process up.

qs.q:
mutation: A mutation is a small random change in a living thing’s instructions. Some mutations let a bacterium survive a drug.
resistant: Resistant means able to survive something that would normally kill it.
Describe the connection between stopping a prescription early and stronger bacteria.
qs.a: Because the weakest bacteria die first, quitting once you feel better leaves the hardiest ones alive, and those are the bacteria that rebuild the infection and pass on their resistance.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you find a record of every year it lived. Each ring is one growing season, and the rings are not all alike.

hi.label: B
hi.text: A tree grows by adding a layer just under the bark. In spring, when water is plentiful, it produces large thin-walled cells that look pale. Later in the season growth slows and the cells are small and dense, forming a dark band. One pale layer plus one dark band equals one year.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The width of a ring records the conditions of that year. A wet year with a long season leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. A scar in the ring records a fire that the tree survived.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The science of reading these records is called dendrochronology. Because every region shares the same weather, trees in one area produce the same distinctive sequence of wide and narrow rings, like a barcode. Researchers can match the outer rings of a living tree to the inner rings of an older dead one, then to a beam in an ancient building, extending the record backward thousands of years.

hi.label: E
hi.text: This is how archaeologists date a wooden roof beam to an exact year rather than a rough century.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Trees in the tropics are less useful. Where there is no winter, growth never pauses, and no clear rings form.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you find a record of every year it lived. Each ring is one growing season.

lo.label: B
lo.text: A tree grows by adding a layer just under the bark. In spring the cells are large and pale. Later in the year they are small and dark. One pale layer plus one dark band equals one year.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The width of a ring records that year. A wet year leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. A scar records a fire the tree lived through.

lo.label: D

lo.label: E
lo.text: This is how a wooden beam can be dated to an exact year.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Tropical trees are less useful. With no winter, growth never pauses and no clear rings form.

qs.q: Explain how one year shows up in a tree trunk.
qs.a: In spring the tree makes large, pale, thin-walled cells, and later in the season it makes small, dense, dark cells. One pale layer plus one dark band is one year of growth.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. weather) and paragraph D (i.e. matching).
Summarize how tree rings let researchers date old wood.
qs.a: Each ring is one year, and its width records that year’s weather, so trees in one region share a distinctive pattern of wide and narrow rings. Researchers match the rings of a living tree to an older dead tree, then to a beam in an ancient building, extending the record back thousands of years.

qs.q:
dendrochronology: Dendrochronology is the science of dating events by studying the rings in trees.
sequence: A sequence is a set of things in a particular order. The order of wide and narrow rings works like a barcode.
Describe the connection between a region having no winter and its trees having no rings.
qs.a: Because rings form when growth slows in a cold or dry season, a tropical tree that grows steadily all year never makes the dark dense band that marks the end of a year.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Electricity is the only major product that is consumed the instant it is made. There is almost no warehouse for it. Supply has to match demand second by second, all day, forever.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Power leaves a plant as alternating current and immediately enters a transformer that raises the voltage, sometimes above 300,000 volts. High voltage is not about power; it is about loss. Pushing the same energy at higher voltage means less current in the wire, and less current means less energy wasted as heat over long distances.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Near your town, substations step the voltage back down in stages, and a final transformer on a pole or pad drops it to the 120 volts in your outlet.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The whole network has to hold a steady frequency of 60 cycles per second. When demand rises, generators are pulled slightly slower and the frequency dips. Operators watch that number constantly and add generation to hold it.

hi.label: E
hi.text: This is why a blackout can cascade. If one line fails, its load shifts to neighboring lines, which may overload and shut down in turn, shifting still more load. In 2003 a single overloaded line in Ohio touched off a chain that darkened parts of eight states in about eight minutes.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The grid is not one machine. It is thousands of machines forced to stay in step with each other.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Electricity is used the instant it is made. There is almost no way to store it. Supply has to match demand second by second.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Power leaves a plant and goes straight into a transformer that raises the voltage very high. High voltage means less current in the wire, and less current means less energy wasted as heat over long distances.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Near your town, substations step the voltage back down. A final transformer on a pole drops it to the 120 volts in your outlet.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The whole network has to hold a steady frequency of 60 cycles a second. When demand rises, the frequency dips, and operators add power to hold it steady.

lo.label: E
lo.text: This is why a blackout can spread. If one line fails, its load shifts to other lines, which may overload and shut down too. In 2003 one overloaded line in Ohio darkened parts of eight states in about eight minutes.

qs.q: Explain why power is sent at very high voltage.
qs.a: Pushing the same energy at higher voltage means less current in the wire, and less current wastes less energy as heat over long distances.

qs.q: Paragraph D (i.e. frequency) and paragraph E (i.e. cascade).
Summarize how electricity gets from a power plant to an outlet.
qs.a: Power leaves the plant and a transformer raises the voltage so less energy is lost as heat on the way. Substations near town step it back down in stages, and a final transformer drops it to 120 volts. Throughout, operators hold the frequency at 60 cycles per second by matching supply to demand.

qs.q:
transformer: A transformer is a device that raises or lowers the voltage of electricity.
cascade: A cascade is a failure that spreads from one part to the next, each one triggering the following.
Describe the connection between one failed line and a blackout across eight states.
qs.a: Because the failed line’s load shifts onto neighboring lines, those lines overload and shut down too, passing still more load along, so one failure spreads through the network in minutes.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Every ten years the United States tries to count every person living in the country. Not citizens. Not voters. Everyone.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The count is written into the Constitution, and it decides how the 435 seats in the House of Representatives are divided among the states. A state that grows faster than its neighbors gains seats. A state that grows slower loses them, even if its population went up.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Money follows the count too. Federal programs distribute hundreds of billions of dollars each year using census figures, so an undercount in one county means fewer dollars for its roads, clinics, and school lunches for a full decade.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Getting an accurate count is harder than it sounds. Some households never return the form, so census takers visit in person. Some people are difficult to reach at a fixed address, and some are counted twice, such as college students recorded both at school and at home.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The Census Bureau estimates its own error afterward by comparing results against a separate survey. Historically, young children, renters, and rural residents have been undercounted.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Individual answers are confidential by law for seventy-two years. That is why genealogists can read the 1950 census in full, but not the most recent one.

lo.label: E

lo.label: F

qs.q: Explain why a state can lose House seats even when its population grows.
qs.a: The 435 seats are divided among the states by comparison, so what matters is how fast a state grows relative to the others. A state that grows more slowly than its neighbors loses seats even though it gained people.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. funding) and paragraph D (i.e. difficulty).
Summarize why the census matters and why it is hard to get right.
qs.a: The census decides how House seats are divided and how hundreds of billions of federal dollars are distributed for a decade. It is hard to get right because some households never return the form, some people are hard to reach, and others are counted twice, so children, renters, and rural residents are often undercounted.

qs.q:
undercount: An undercount is a count lower than the real number. An undercounted county loses funding for ten years.
confidential: Confidential means kept private. Individual census answers stay confidential for seventy-two years.
Describe the connection between an undercount and a county’s schools.
qs.a: Because federal money is handed out using census figures, a county counted short receives fewer dollars for every year until the next census, which reaches programs like school lunches.

hi.label: A
hi.text: The problem was invisible. Lead does not change the color, smell, or taste of water, and in small amounts it does not make anyone immediately sick. It accumulates in the body over years, and in children it damages the developing brain.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The source was the pipes themselves. Lead service lines, the pipe running from the street main into a house, were standard in American cities until 1986. Millions are still in the ground.

hi.label: C
hi.text: For decades the solution was chemical rather than physical. Utilities added orthophosphate to the water, which coats the inside of the pipe with a mineral film. Water then touches the film instead of the lead.

hi.label: D
hi.text: That solution has a weakness: it only works if nothing disturbs the film. In 2014 Flint, Michigan switched water sources without adding corrosion control. The new water stripped the coating, and lead began entering homes within weeks.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Residents reported discolored water and rashes. Officials said the water met standards. Independent testing by a Virginia Tech team and a local pediatrician’s review of children’s blood tests eventually forced the city to reverse course.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The lasting solution is the expensive one: dig up the lines and replace them. Cities are now doing it, at a cost measured in billions and a timeline measured in decades.

lo.text: The problem was invisible. Lead does not change the color, smell, or taste of water. It builds up in the body over years, and in children it damages the growing brain.

lo.label: C

lo.label: D

lo.label: E

lo.label: F
lo.text: The lasting fix is the expensive one: dig up the pipes and replace them.

qs.q: Explain why the chemical coating was only a partial solution.
qs.a: The coating works only as long as nothing disturbs it. When Flint switched water sources without corrosion control, the new water stripped the film away and lead entered homes within weeks.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. coating) and paragraph F (i.e. replacement).
Summarize the problem and the solutions described.
qs.a: Lead service lines, standard until 1986, leach lead into drinking water where it cannot be seen or tasted. Utilities coated the pipes chemically, which works only while the film stays intact. Flint stripped that film in 2014. The lasting solution is digging up and replacing the lines.

accumulates: Accumulates means builds up little by little over time.
corrosion: Corrosion is the slow eating away of metal. Corrosion control keeps water from stripping the pipe.

qs.a: Because lead does not change how water looks, smells, or tastes, and causes no immediate illness, families kept drinking it for years while the damage accumulated unnoticed.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A gasoline car and an electric car do the same job by opposite methods. Comparing them part by part shows where each one wins.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Start with the engine. A gasoline engine has hundreds of moving parts and converts roughly a quarter of the fuel’s energy into motion; the rest becomes heat. An electric motor has about a dozen moving parts and converts most of its energy into motion.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Refueling flips the advantage. A gasoline tank fills in five minutes anywhere in the country. Charging a battery takes twenty minutes on the fastest chargers and many hours on a household outlet.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Maintenance favors electric again. No oil changes, no spark plugs, no exhaust system. Brakes last longer because the motor does much of the slowing.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Manufacturing favors gasoline. Building a battery takes mining lithium, nickel, and cobalt, and an electric car leaves the factory with a larger carbon footprint than a gasoline car does.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Over a lifetime, the picture reverses again. Most studies find an electric car makes up its manufacturing deficit within one to two years of driving and emits less overall after that, though how much less depends on how the local electricity is generated.

lo.text: A gasoline car and an electric car do the same job in opposite ways. Comparing them part by part shows where each one wins.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Start with the engine. A gasoline engine has hundreds of moving parts and turns about a quarter of the fuel into motion. An electric motor has about a dozen and turns most of its energy into motion.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Refueling flips it. A gas tank fills in five minutes anywhere. Charging takes twenty minutes on a fast charger and many hours at home.

lo.label: D

lo.label: E

lo.label: F

qs.q: Explain why an electric car starts out with a larger carbon footprint.
qs.a: Building its battery requires mining lithium, nickel, and cobalt, so the car has already caused more emissions by the time it leaves the factory than a gasoline car has.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. refueling) and paragraph E (i.e. manufacturing).

qs.a: The electric motor is simpler and wastes far less energy, and an electric car needs less maintenance. Gasoline wins on refueling speed and on manufacturing, since battery materials must be mined. Over one to two years of driving, the electric car makes up that deficit and emits less overall.

efficiency: Efficiency is how much of the energy put in actually does useful work.
footprint: A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gas something causes to be released.
Describe the connection between where electricity comes from and how clean an electric car is.
qs.a: Because an electric car runs on power from the grid, its emissions depend on how that power was generated, so the same car is cleaner in a region using wind or hydro than one burning coal.

hi.label: A
hi.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted with more force than any volcano in recorded history. The explosion was heard sixteen hundred miles away.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The eruption threw an enormous quantity of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, far above the weather. There it formed a haze of tiny droplets that reflected sunlight back into space. Because the stratosphere has no rain to wash particles out, the haze spread worldwide and stayed for years.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Global temperatures fell roughly one degree Fahrenheit. That sounds trivial. It was enough to shorten growing seasons across the Northern Hemisphere.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The following year, 1816, became known as the year without a summer. Snow fell in New England in June. Frost killed crops in August. Grain prices in Europe doubled, and famine followed in Ireland, Switzerland, and parts of China.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The effects reached beyond hunger. Thousands of New England families gave up and moved west, accelerating the settlement of Indiana and Illinois. In Switzerland, a group of writers kept indoors by relentless rain held a contest to write ghost stories. One of them, eighteen years old, wrote Frankenstein.

hi.label: F
hi.text: A single mountain, on the far side of the world, changed what people ate, where they lived, and what they wrote, for years afterward.

lo.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted with more force than any volcano in recorded history. The explosion was heard sixteen hundred miles away.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The eruption threw sulfur gas high above the weather. There it formed a haze that reflected sunlight back into space. With no rain that high to wash it out, the haze spread worldwide and stayed for years.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Temperatures fell about one degree. That sounds small. It was enough to shorten growing seasons across the north.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The next year, 1816, became known as the year without a summer. Snow fell in New England in June. Frost killed crops in August. Grain prices doubled and famine followed.

lo.label: E

lo.label: F
lo.text: One mountain changed what people ate, where they lived, and what they wrote.

qs.q: Explain why the haze from one eruption lasted for years.
qs.a: The sulfur reached the stratosphere, above the weather. Because there is no rain that high to wash particles out, the haze spread around the globe and stayed aloft for years.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. cooling) and paragraph E (i.e. consequences).
Summarize the chain of effects from the eruption.
qs.a: Tambora erupted in 1815 and threw sulfur into the stratosphere, where it formed a haze that reflected sunlight. Global temperatures fell about one degree, shortening growing seasons. Crops failed in 1816, grain prices doubled, famine spread, families migrated west, and a rainy Swiss summer produced Frankenstein.

qs.q:

hi.text: A lock is a concrete chamber with a gate at each end. A boat headed upstream enters through the lower gate, which then closes behind it. The chamber is now sealed, holding the boat at the lower water level.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Valves in the upper gate open. Water from the higher stretch of canal flows in by gravity alone. The water level in the chamber rises, and the boat rises with it, floating the whole time.

hi.label: D
hi.text: When the chamber water matches the upper canal, the pressure on both sides of the upper gate is equal. Only then will the gate swing open. The boat motors out at the higher level, and the lock is ready for the next one.

hi.label: E
hi.text: A boat going downstream runs the same steps in reverse, draining instead of filling. Each cycle uses a chamber of water, which is why locks on a busy canal are often built in pairs so one can fill while the other empties.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The Panama Canal lifts ships 85 feet using three sets of locks. The physics is the same as a canal lock in Ohio. Only the scale is different.

Seeing the five stages together makes the sequence and the reason for the order clear.

qs.q:
chamber: A chamber is an enclosed space. In a lock it is the concrete box between the two gates.
gravity: Gravity is the force pulling things down. It moves the water into the lock without a pump.
Describe the connection between equal pressure and the gate opening.
qs.a: Because water pushes hard against a gate when the levels are different, the gate cannot be forced open. Once the chamber has filled to match the upper canal, the push is the same on both sides and the gate swings freely.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Three days before a hurricane reaches land, forecasters publish a map with a cone on it. The cone is the single most misread graphic in American weather reporting.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The cone does not show the size of the storm. It shows where the center of the storm might travel. Historically, the true center stays inside the cone about two thirds of the time.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The cone widens with time because forecasts get less certain the farther out they reach. At 12 hours the cone is narrow. At 120 hours it can be hundreds of miles across.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Damaging wind and rain routinely occur far outside the cone. A town 150 miles from the drawn line can flood while a town on the line stays dry. The line is a probability, not a promise.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Forecasters also publish a separate surge map and a wind-arrival map. Emergency managers use those, not the cone, when they decide whether to order evacuations.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The cone remains in public forecasts because people understand a line better than they understand a probability. Whether that trade is worth making is still argued.

lo.text: Three days before a hurricane reaches land, forecasters publish a map with a cone on it. The cone is the most misread graphic in weather reporting.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The cone does not show how big the storm is. It shows where the center of the storm might go. The real center stays inside the cone about two thirds of the time.

lo.label: C

lo.label: D

lo.label: E

lo.label: F
lo.text: The cone stays in public forecasts because people understand a line better than a probability.

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why the cone gets wider farther into the future.
qs.a: The chart shows the cone growing from about 30 miles at 12 hours to more than 300 miles at 120 hours. It widens because a forecast is less certain the farther ahead it reaches, so the range of places the center could be gets larger.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. misreading) and paragraph E (i.e. deciding).
Explain how the chart changes what you understand about paragraph D.
qs.a: Paragraph D says damage happens far outside the cone. The chart explains why: the cone only tracks the center, and its last row states plainly that it shows nothing about storm size, wind reach, rainfall, or surge. Together they show that being outside the line is not the same as being safe.

qs.q:
probability: A probability is how likely something is, not a guarantee that it will happen.
surge: Storm surge is ocean water pushed inland by a storm, which floods the coast.
Describe the connection between the cone showing only the center and people misreading it.
qs.a: Because the drawn cone looks like the outline of the storm, readers assume everything inside is dangerous and everything outside is safe, when the cone only marks where the center might pass.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A cheetah can reach 70 miles per hour. That number appears on posters and in trivia books, and by itself it explains almost nothing about how a cheetah hunts.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The cheetah holds that speed for roughly twenty seconds. After that its body temperature rises past what it can safely carry, and it must stop. Most chases end in under a minute whether or not the cheetah has caught anything.

hi.label: C
hi.text: A pronghorn antelope tops out slower, near 55 miles per hour, but can hold 30 miles per hour for many miles. It evolved alongside a predator that no longer exists, and it is now faster than anything that chases it.

hi.label: D
hi.text: An ostrich runs about 43 miles per hour and can sustain it far longer than a cheetah. A greyhound reaches 45 but tires quickly, much like the cheetah.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Comparing only top speed puts the cheetah first every time. Comparing distance held at speed puts the pronghorn first and moves the cheetah to last.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Neither ranking is wrong. They measure different things, which is why a single number about an animal is rarely enough.

lo.label: B

lo.label: C

lo.label: D

lo.label: F

qs.q: Use the graph to explain why the cheetah is both first and last.
qs.a: The graph ranks the animals two ways. By top speed the cheetah leads at 70 mph. By how long that speed is held, the cheetah manages about twenty seconds while the pronghorn keeps 30 mph for miles, so the cheetah drops to last.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. overheating) and paragraph E (i.e. comparing).
Explain how the graph supports the point made in paragraph F.
qs.a: Paragraph F says the two rankings measure different things and neither is wrong. The graph shows this directly by placing top speed and distance held side by side, so the same four animals come out in nearly opposite orders depending on which column you read.

qs.q:
sustain: To sustain a speed is to keep it going over time instead of only reaching it briefly.
evolved: Evolved means changed slowly over many generations to survive in a particular place.
Describe the connection between the cheetah’s body temperature and the length of its chases.
qs.a: Because sprinting heats the cheetah’s body faster than it can cool, it must stop after roughly twenty seconds, so its hunts are decided in under a minute whether or not it catches anything.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A city receives rain the same way a field does. What happens next is not the same at all.

hi.label: B
hi.text: In a meadow, most rain soaks into the ground. Roots slow it, soil holds it, and it reaches the stream over hours or days. Only a small share runs off the surface.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Under a parking lot, none of that happens. Asphalt absorbs nothing. Rain hits it and moves immediately toward the nearest drain, arriving in the creek within minutes rather than hours.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The total amount of water is unchanged. The timing is what changes. A creek that would have risen slowly over a day instead rises sharply in twenty minutes, which is what causes flash flooding downstream.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Cities now build rain gardens, permeable pavement, and detention basins to delay runoff on purpose. None of these reduce the rainfall. They spread its arrival out again.

hi.label: F
hi.text: A city block with 20 percent of its surface paved behaves like a meadow. At 60 percent paved, it behaves like a roof.

lo.label: A
lo.text: A city gets rain the same way a field does. What happens next is not the same.

lo.label: B
lo.text: In a meadow, most rain soaks into the ground. Roots slow it and soil holds it. It reaches the stream over hours or days.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Under a parking lot, none of that happens. Asphalt soaks up nothing. Rain hits it and runs to the nearest drain, reaching the creek in minutes.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The amount of water is the same. The timing changes. A creek that would rise slowly over a day instead rises fast in twenty minutes, which causes flash flooding.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Cities now build rain gardens and special pavement to slow runoff on purpose. These do not reduce the rain. They spread out when it arrives.

lo.label: F
lo.text: A block with 20 percent paved acts like a meadow. At 60 percent paved, it acts like a roof.

qs.q: Use the graph to explain why the same storm floods a city but not a meadow.
qs.a: The graph shows a meadow absorbing about 90 of every 100 drops and releasing the rest over hours or days, while a parking lot absorbs almost none and sends nearly all of it to the creek within minutes. The rainfall is identical; the speed of arrival is what floods the city.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. runoff) and paragraph E (i.e. delaying).
Explain how the graph adds to what paragraph D tells you.
qs.a: Paragraph D states that the total water is unchanged and only the timing differs. The graph shows both halves of that at once: the soaks-in and runs-off rows account for the same inch of rain either way, and the last row shows the difference is hours versus minutes.

qs.q:
permeable: Permeable means able to let water pass through. Permeable pavement lets rain soak in.
detention: A detention basin is a dip in the ground that holds runoff for a while before releasing it.
Describe the connection between paved ground and flash flooding downstream.
qs.a: Because pavement sends rain to the drains at once instead of letting soil release it slowly, the creek receives a whole storm in twenty minutes and rises faster than its channel can carry, which floods the land below.

g4-34.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "asphalt absorbs nothing" or "at 60 percent paved a block behaves like a roof." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Ask which bridge is the longest and you will get four different answers, all of them correct.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China runs 102 miles. Almost all of it crosses farmland and rice paddies on short concrete spans. It is the longest bridge of any kind.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan has a main span of 6,532 feet. That is the distance between its two towers with nothing underneath. No bridge holds a longer single gap.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana stretches almost 24 miles over open water, the longest continuous bridge across water anywhere.

hi.label: E
hi.text: These are three different measurements: total length, longest single span, and length over water. A bridge can lead one list and not appear on another.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The main span matters most to engineers, because the gap a bridge can cross without a support is the hard problem. Total length is mostly a question of how many identical spans you are willing to pay for.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Ask which bridge is the longest and you will get four different answers, all correct.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China runs 102 miles. Almost all of it crosses farmland on short concrete spans. It is the longest bridge of any kind.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan has a main span of 6,532 feet. That is the gap between its two towers with nothing underneath. No bridge has a longer single gap.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana runs almost 24 miles over open water. That is the longest bridge across water anywhere.

lo.label: E
lo.text: These are three different measurements: total length, longest single span, and length over water. A bridge can lead one list and miss another.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Engineers care most about the main span, because crossing a gap without a support is the hard problem.

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why the longest bridge is not the hardest to build.
qs.a: The chart shows Danyang–Kunshan leading total length at 102 miles, but its length comes from joining many short spans. The hardest measurement is the main span, where Akashi Kaikyo leads with 6,532 feet of gap that nothing supports in the middle.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. repeating) and paragraph F (i.e. engineering).
Explain how the chart makes paragraph E easier to understand.
qs.a: Paragraph E says there are three different measurements and a bridge can lead one list without appearing on another. The chart shows that directly: three different bridges in three different countries hold the three records, and no name repeats.

qs.q:
span: A span is the distance a bridge crosses between two supports.
causeway: A causeway is a raised road or bridge built across water or wet ground.
Describe the connection between building supports and how long a bridge can be.
qs.a: Because a bridge resting on many supports can simply repeat the same short span as far as the budget allows, total length is a matter of cost, while the span between two towers is limited by what the structure itself can hold up.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Most American middle schools begin before 8:00 a.m. They should begin after 8:30, and the reasons have little to do with whether students are willing to go to bed.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The first reason is biological. At puberty the body clock shifts later by about two hours. A thirteen-year-old told to sleep at 9:00 p.m. is being asked to fall asleep at what her body reads as 7:00. This shift is measurable in hormone levels and is not a matter of discipline.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The second reason is safety. Crash rates for teenage drivers fall when start times move later. One district that shifted from 7:20 to 8:40 recorded 70 percent fewer teen crashes in the following two years.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The third reason is academic. Schools that delayed start times report higher attendance and fewer first-period failures. The gains are largest for students who ride the earliest buses.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The usual objection is athletics and bus scheduling. Both are real costs. Districts that made the change solved them by running buses in a different order and moving practice to mornings for some teams.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Costs that can be scheduled around are not the same as reasons to keep a start time that fights student biology every morning.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Most middle schools start before 8:00 a.m. They should start after 8:30, and the reasons have little to do with bedtime rules.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The first reason is biology. At puberty the body clock shifts about two hours later. A thirteen-year-old told to sleep at 9:00 p.m. is being asked to sleep at what her body reads as 7:00.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The second reason is safety. Teen crash rates drop when start times move later. One district moved from 7:20 to 8:40 and had 70 percent fewer teen crashes.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The third reason is school work. Schools that started later report better attendance and fewer first-period failures. The biggest gains go to students on the earliest buses.

lo.label: E
lo.text: The usual objection is sports and buses. Both are real costs. Districts fixed them by running buses in a different order and moving some practices to mornings.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Costs you can schedule around are not the same as reasons to keep a start time that fights student biology.

qs.q: Which reason has the strongest evidence behind it, and why?
qs.a: The safety reason. It offers a specific number from a specific district: a shift from 7:20 to 8:40 followed by 70 percent fewer teen crashes over two years. The academic reason reports a direction but gives no figures.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. biology) and paragraph E (i.e. objection).
Explain how the author uses reasons and evidence to support the claim.
qs.a: The author states the claim in paragraph A, then gives three reasons in order: a biological shift measurable in hormones, a crash-rate drop of 70 percent in one district, and better attendance with fewer first-period failures. Paragraph E then names the strongest objection and shows how districts solved it, so the claim is left standing.

qs.q:
biological: Biological means having to do with how a living body works, not with choices a person makes.
objection: An objection is a reason someone gives against an idea.
Describe the connection between the body clock shifting and an early start time being hard.
qs.a: Because puberty moves the body clock about two hours later, a teenager cannot fall asleep at the hour an early start requires, so the early bell costs sleep no matter what time she goes to bed.

hi.label: A
hi.text: The city council has proposed closing the public library on Sundays to save money. The proposal would save less than it appears to and cost more than it admits.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Start with the savings. Sunday hours cost the library about $41,000 a year, which is under one percent of its budget. Closing would not solve the shortfall the council is trying to close.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Now the use. Sunday is the branch’s second-busiest day. The circulation desk counts an average of 610 visitors, compared with 380 on a typical Tuesday. Those visitors are not distributed evenly: most arrive between noon and 4:00.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Sunday is also the only day many patrons can come. Of the adults surveyed at the door, 44 percent said they work weekdays and cannot reach the library before it closes at 6:00.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The council argues that the bookmobile can absorb the demand. The bookmobile holds roughly 800 items and has no computers, no study rooms, and no staff librarian. The branch holds 94,000 items.

hi.label: F
hi.text: A one percent saving that removes the busiest access day for working adults is not a saving. It is a shift of the cost onto the people who have the fewest alternatives.

lo.label: F

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls the bookmobile an inadequate replacement.

Explain how the author uses reasons and evidence to argue against the closure.

circulation: Circulation is the counting and lending of library items, and the desk where that happens.
patrons: Patrons are the people who use a library or other public service.
Describe the connection between weekday work hours and Sunday library use.
qs.a: Because 44 percent of adults surveyed work while the library is open on weekdays, Sunday is the only day they can get there, which is why the second-busiest day would vanish rather than move.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Cities that ban thin plastic grocery bags usually expect two results: less plastic in landfills and fewer bags in waterways. The first result is not what happens.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The reason is substitution. When the thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker reusable plastic bags and, separately, more small trash-can liners. A thin grocery bag weighs about 5 grams. A thick reusable plastic bag weighs about 80 grams.

hi.label: C
hi.text: One study of a large California ban found that plastic bag weight dropped by 40 million pounds a year, and that purchases of trash bags rose by 12 million pounds in the same area. The net reduction was real but far smaller than the headline number.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The second result, however, holds up. Litter surveys after bans consistently find fewer plastic bags in storm drains, on beaches, and in the stomachs of seabirds and turtles. A thicker bag that gets reused does not blow into a creek.

hi.label: E
hi.text: So the honest case for a bag ban is not mainly about landfill volume. It is about what escapes the waste stream, where a 5-gram bag does damage out of all proportion to its weight.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Arguing for the wrong reason is risky. When the landfill claim fails, opponents use the failure to dismiss the litter evidence, which is the stronger part of the case.

lo.text: Cities that ban thin plastic grocery bags expect two results: less plastic in landfills and fewer bags in waterways. The first one does not happen.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The reason is substitution. When thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker reusable bags and more small trash-can liners. A thin bag weighs about 5 grams. A thick reusable bag weighs about 80 grams.

lo.label: C
lo.text: One study of a large California ban found plastic bag weight dropped by 40 million pounds a year, while trash bag purchases rose by 12 million pounds. The real drop was much smaller than the headline.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The second result holds up. Litter surveys after bans find fewer bags in storm drains, on beaches, and in the stomachs of seabirds and turtles.

lo.label: E
lo.text: So the honest case for a bag ban is not about landfill volume. It is about what escapes into the environment, where a 5-gram bag does great damage.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Arguing for the wrong reason is risky. When the landfill claim fails, opponents use it to dismiss the litter evidence, which is stronger.

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls Claim A weakened.
qs.a: The ban removed 40 million pounds of bag plastic but shoppers bought 12 million pounds more trash bags, and the replacement bags weigh about 80 grams against 5 grams. The reduction is real but much smaller than the headline figure suggests.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. substitution) and paragraph D (i.e. litter).
Explain how the author treats the two reasons differently.
qs.a: The author tests each reason against evidence. The landfill reason is weakened by the study showing trash-bag purchases rising and by the weight comparison between a 5-gram bag and an 80-gram one. The litter reason is supported by consistent survey findings in drains, on beaches, and in wildlife, so the author keeps it and drops the other.

qs.q:
substitution: Substitution is replacing one thing with another. Here, shoppers replace thin bags with thicker ones.
net: A net amount is what is left after gains and losses are counted together.
Describe the connection between arguing a weak reason and losing a strong one.
qs.a: Because opponents can disprove the landfill claim with the trash-bag numbers, they can then treat the whole argument as unreliable, and the litter evidence that the data does support gets dismissed along with it.

hi.label: A
hi.text: In many schools recess is withheld as a punishment for unfinished work or misbehavior. The practice takes the thing a struggling student most needs and removes it exactly when it is needed.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Consider what recess does. Physical activity raises blood flow to the brain and improves attention on the task that follows. Studies of elementary classrooms find measurable gains in on-task behavior in the twenty minutes after a break.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Now consider who loses recess. It is rarely the student who finished early. The students who lose it most often are the ones with attention difficulties, which is the group whose attention improves the most from movement.

hi.label: D
hi.text: There is also a fairness problem. Recess is the only part of the school day that is not academic, so taking it removes a student’s only chance to practice negotiating, taking turns, and settling a dispute without an adult.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Teachers who stop using recess as leverage need a replacement, and the honest answer is that consequences take longer that way. A conversation costs more minutes than a withheld recess.

hi.label: F
hi.text: But the minutes are spent on the problem instead of on making the next hour of the day harder for everyone in the room.

lo.label: A
lo.text: In many schools recess is taken away as a punishment for unfinished work. The practice removes the thing a struggling student most needs, right when it is needed.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Consider what recess does. Moving raises blood flow to the brain and improves attention on the next task. Studies find real gains in on-task behavior in the twenty minutes after a break.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Now consider who loses recess. It is rarely the student who finished early. It is most often students with attention difficulties, the group that gains most from movement.

lo.label: D
lo.text: There is also a fairness problem. Recess is the only part of the day that is not academic. Taking it removes a student’s only chance to practice taking turns and settling a dispute without an adult.

lo.label: E

lo.label: F
lo.text: But those minutes are spent on the problem instead of making the next hour harder for everyone.

qs.a: Reason 1 says attention improves in the twenty minutes after a break, and Reason 2 says the students who lose recess most often are those with attention difficulties. So recess is taken from exactly the students whose attention it would help most.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. mismatch) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Explain how the author supports the claim and handles the cost of it.
qs.a: The author gives three reasons: movement improves on-task behavior afterward, the students who lose recess are the ones who benefit most, and recess is the only non-academic time in the day. Paragraph E then admits the real cost, that a conversation takes longer than a withheld recess, and argues the minutes are better spent.

qs.q:
leverage: Leverage is something you hold over a person to make them do what you want.
negotiating: Negotiating is working out an agreement with someone by talking it through.
Describe the connection between physical activity and the work that follows a break.
qs.a: Because moving raises blood flow to the brain, students return to their seats better able to hold attention, so the twenty minutes after recess are measurably more productive than the same minutes without it.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A team owner has asked the city for $180 million toward a new stadium, promising jobs and downtown business. Nearly every study of past stadium deals says the promise does not arrive.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The jobs argument comes first. Stadium construction does create work, but it ends. Permanent stadium jobs are mostly part-time and seasonal: ushers, concessions, cleaning. Economists who have reviewed dozens of these deals find no measurable increase in regional employment.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The spending argument is the weaker one. Money spent at a game is not new money. A family that buys tickets is a family that did not spend that evening at a restaurant or a bowling alley in the same city. The dollars move; they do not multiply.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The cost, meanwhile, is fixed and public. $180 million is roughly what this city spends on street maintenance in nine years.

hi.label: E
hi.text: There is a genuine argument on the other side, and it is not economic. A team can be part of how a city sees itself, and that is worth something real that no study measures well.

hi.label: F
hi.text: A city may reasonably decide to pay for that. It should decide knowing it is buying identity, not jobs.

lo.label: A
lo.text: A team owner has asked the city for $180 million toward a new stadium, promising jobs and downtown business. Nearly every study of past deals says the promise does not arrive.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The jobs argument comes first. Building a stadium does create work, but it ends. Permanent stadium jobs are mostly part-time: ushers, concessions, cleaning. Economists find no real rise in regional jobs.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The spending argument is weaker. Money spent at a game is not new money. A family that buys tickets did not spend that evening at a restaurant in the same city. The dollars move; they do not multiply.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The cost is fixed and public. $180 million is about what this city spends on street repair in nine years.

lo.label: E
lo.text: There is a real argument on the other side, and it is not about money. A team can be part of how a city sees itself.

lo.label: F
lo.text: A city may decide to pay for that. It should decide knowing it is buying identity, not jobs.

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls the spending promise the weaker one.
qs.a: Money spent at a game is not new money. A family buying tickets is not spending that evening at a local restaurant or bowling alley, so the dollars shift between businesses in the same city rather than adding up to more.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. shifting) and paragraph E (i.e. identity).
Explain how the author uses evidence to separate the strong argument from the weak ones.
qs.a: The author tests each promise. Jobs fail because construction work ends and permanent positions are part-time, with economists finding no regional gain. New spending fails because ticket dollars move from other local businesses. The $180 million cost is compared to nine years of street maintenance. Only the civic-identity argument survives, and the author concedes it is not economic.

qs.q:
permanent: Permanent means lasting. A permanent job continues after construction is finished.
civic: Civic means having to do with a city and the people who live in it.
Describe the connection between a family buying tickets and a nearby restaurant losing business.
qs.a: Because a family has one evening and one entertainment budget, the money it spends at the stadium is money it does not spend at a restaurant or bowling alley nearby, so the city’s total spending stays about the same.
