hi.label: A
hi.text: TEXT 1 · From a park history. Wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone by 1926. For nearly seventy years the park had none. In 1995 and 1996, fourteen wolves from Canada were released into the Lamar Valley.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The elk population had grown to roughly 19,000 and was browsing young willow and aspen faster than the trees could grow. Streambanks, held together by those roots, were collapsing.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Within fifteen years the elk herd fell by more than half. Willow returned along several creeks. Beaver colonies, which had dropped to one, rose to nine.

hi.label: D
hi.text: TEXT 2 · From an ecologist’s essay. The Yellowstone wolf story is usually told as a chain: wolves ate elk, willows grew back, rivers healed. The chain is real in places and overstated everywhere else.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Elk numbers fell partly from wolves and partly from drought, bear predation on calves, and a deliberate increase in hunting outside the park. Assigning the whole drop to wolves ignores three other pressures acting at once.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Willow recovery also varied. Where groundwater stayed high, willow returned strongly. Where it did not, willow stayed short even with no elk browsing. Wolves changed the system. They did not run it alone.

lo.label: A
lo.text: TEXT 1 · From a park history. Wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone by 1926. For nearly seventy years the park had none. In 1995 and 1996, fourteen wolves from Canada were released there.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The elk had grown to about 19,000 and were eating young willow and aspen faster than the trees could grow. Streambanks held by those roots were falling in.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Within fifteen years the elk herd fell by more than half. Willow came back along several creeks. Beaver colonies rose from one to nine.

lo.label: D
lo.text: TEXT 2 · From an ecologist’s essay. The wolf story is usually told as a chain: wolves ate elk, willows grew back, rivers healed. The chain is real in some places and overstated in others.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Elk numbers fell partly from wolves and partly from drought, bears eating calves, and more hunting outside the park. Giving wolves all the credit ignores three other causes.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Willow recovery varied too. Where groundwater stayed high, willow grew back strongly. Where it did not, willow stayed short even with no elk. Wolves changed the system, but not alone.

qs.q: Using both texts, explain why the elk population fell.
qs.a: Text 1 shows the herd dropping by more than half after wolves returned. Text 2 adds that drought, bears preying on calves, and increased hunting outside the park were acting at the same time, so wolves were one cause among several rather than the only one.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. recovery) and paragraph E (i.e. causes).
Combine both texts into an accurate summary of what wolves did to Yellowstone.
qs.a: Fourteen wolves were returned in 1995 and 1996 to a park that had none since 1926, where 19,000 elk were browsing willow faster than it grew. The herd then fell by more than half, willow returned along several creeks, and beaver colonies rose from one to nine. The second text shows the drop also owed to drought, bear predation, and hunting, and that willow only recovered fully where groundwater stayed high.

qs.q:
predation: Predation is one animal hunting and eating another.
groundwater: Groundwater is water held in the soil below the surface, which plant roots reach.
Describe the connection between elk browsing and collapsing streambanks.
qs.a: Because elk ate young willow faster than it could grow, the roots that held the soil along the creeks never developed, and the banks lost the structure that kept them from falling in.

g4-41.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "beaver colonies rose from one to nine" or "willow stayed short where groundwater was low." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

hi.label: A
hi.text: TEXT 1 · From a school history. In 1587, about 115 English colonists settled on Roanoke Island. Their governor, John White, sailed back to England for supplies that same year.

hi.label: B
hi.text: War with Spain delayed his return for three years. When White finally landed in 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down carefully rather than burned.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The word CROATOAN was carved into a post. White had arranged in advance that a carved cross would mean the colonists left in distress. There was no cross.

hi.label: D
hi.text: TEXT 2 · From a recent archaeology report. Croatoan was a real place and a real people, on what is now Hatteras Island, fifty miles south. Excavations there have recovered English items in layers dated to the right period.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The finds include a sword hilt, a slate writing tablet with a lead pencil, and fragments of English pottery, mixed with Native tools in the same layer rather than in a separate English area.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Mixed layers suggest people living together rather than trading at a distance. The evidence is suggestive, not conclusive: English goods also moved along trade routes without their owners.

lo.label: A
lo.text: TEXT 1 · From a school history. In 1587, about 115 English colonists settled on Roanoke Island. Their governor, John White, sailed back to England for supplies that year.

lo.label: B
lo.text: War with Spain delayed his return for three years. When White landed in 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down carefully, not burned.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The word CROATOAN was carved into a post. White had arranged that a carved cross would mean the colonists left in danger. There was no cross.

lo.label: D
lo.text: TEXT 2 · From a recent archaeology report. Croatoan was a real place and a real people, on what is now Hatteras Island, fifty miles south. Digs there found English items from the right period.

lo.label: E
lo.text: The finds include a sword hilt, a slate writing tablet with a pencil, and English pottery, mixed with Native tools in the same layer.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Mixed layers suggest people living together, not trading from far away. The evidence is suggestive, not proof: English goods also traveled without their owners.

qs.q: Using both texts, explain why the carved word matters more than it first appears.
qs.a: Text 1 shows CROATOAN carved without the agreed distress cross, suggesting a planned departure to a named place. Text 2 shows Croatoan was a real people on Hatteras Island, where English objects turn up in dated layers, so the carving points somewhere the evidence can be checked.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. signal) and paragraph F (i.e. caution).
Integrate both texts into what can reasonably be said about the colony.
qs.a: About 115 colonists settled Roanoke in 1587 and were gone when their governor returned in 1590, leaving dismantled houses and the word CROATOAN carved without the agreed distress cross. Excavations on Hatteras, once Croatoan, have found a sword hilt, a slate tablet, and English pottery mixed with Native tools in period layers. That fits colonists living among the Croatoan, though trade could also carry such goods.

qs.q:
excavations: Excavations are careful digs made to uncover and study buried objects.
conclusive: Conclusive evidence settles a question. Suggestive evidence only points toward an answer.
Describe the connection between the war with Spain and the colony being lost.
qs.a: Because the war held White in England for three years instead of months, the colonists had to act on their own, and by the time he returned no one remained to explain where they had gone or why.

g4-42.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the houses were taken down rather than burned" or "English goods moved along trade routes." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

hi.label: A
hi.text: TEXT 1 · From a conservation organization. Forty-one species now alive exist only because of zoos. The Arabian oryx was extinct in the wild in 1972 and was returned to the desert from zoo-bred herds.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Accredited zoos contribute about $230 million a year to field conservation. They also hold breeding populations for species whose wild habitat is not currently safe, which buys time that habitat work requires.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Public contact matters as well. Surveys find that visitors leave with greater knowledge of local species and higher stated willingness to support conservation funding.

hi.label: D
hi.text: TEXT 2 · From an animal-welfare researcher. The conservation figures are accurate and describe a small share of what zoos do. Of species held in accredited zoos, fewer than one in ten are part of any reintroduction program.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The welfare question is separate from the conservation question. Elephants in zoos show shortened lifespans and repetitive pacing behaviors. Large carnivores with wide natural ranges fare worst; small, territorial species often fare well.

hi.label: F
hi.text: A defensible zoo is not one that holds every animal a crowd expects. It is one that holds the animals it can house properly and sends the rest of its money into the field.

lo.label: A
lo.text: TEXT 1 · From a conservation group. Forty-one species alive today exist only because of zoos. The Arabian oryx was gone from the wild in 1972 and was returned to the desert from zoo-bred herds.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Accredited zoos give about $230 million a year to field conservation. They also keep breeding groups for species whose wild habitat is not safe yet.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Public contact matters too. Surveys find visitors leave knowing more about local species and more willing to support conservation.

lo.label: D
lo.text: TEXT 2 · From an animal-welfare researcher. Those numbers are accurate and describe a small part of what zoos do. Fewer than one in ten species in accredited zoos are part of any release program.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Welfare is a separate question. Elephants in zoos live shorter lives and pace repeatedly. Large carnivores with wide ranges do worst; small territorial species often do well.

lo.label: F
lo.text: A good zoo is not one that holds every animal a crowd expects. It is one that holds the animals it can house well.

qs.q: Using both texts, explain why the two authors do not actually contradict each other.
qs.a: Text 2 states that Text 1’s conservation figures are accurate. It argues they cover a small share of zoo activity, since fewer than one in ten species are in release programs, and it raises welfare, a separate question that Text 1 never addresses.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. funding) and paragraph E (i.e. welfare).
Integrate both texts into a balanced position on zoos.
qs.a: Zoos have kept 41 species alive, returned the Arabian oryx to the desert, and send about $230 million a year into the field, and visitors leave more willing to support conservation. But fewer than one in ten species held are part of any reintroduction program, and welfare varies sharply: elephants and wide-ranging carnivores do badly while small territorial species do well. The defensible zoo keeps the animals it can house properly.

qs.q:
accredited: An accredited zoo has been inspected and approved against a set of standards.
reintroduction: Reintroduction is returning animals raised in captivity to live in the wild again.
Describe the connection between an animal’s natural range and how it does in a zoo.
qs.a: Because a species that normally travels many miles cannot be given that distance in an enclosure, wide-ranging animals like elephants and large carnivores show pacing and shortened lives, while species that naturally hold a small territory find an enclosure closer to normal.

hi.label: A
hi.text: TEXT 1 · Oral history, recorded 1978. "April 14, 1935. We called it Black Sunday afterward. The morning was clear and warm and people hung wash out."

hi.label: B
hi.text: "The cloud came from the north and it was not a rain cloud. It was two thousand feet high and it was brown. My mother put wet sheets over the windows and it still came in. You could not see a lamp across the room."

hi.label: C
hi.text: "We had six good years on that land before that. People say the farmers should have known. Nobody told us. The government men came out and taught contour plowing in 1937, two years after."

hi.label: D
hi.text: TEXT 2 · From an agricultural history. The southern Plains were grassland whose deep roots held the soil through drought cycles that recurred every twenty years or so.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Between 1925 and 1930, tractor farming broke roughly 5 million acres of that sod for wheat. Wheat roots are shallow and annual. When the drought arrived on schedule in 1931, there was nothing holding the soil.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Federal soil-conservation programs began in 1935 and taught contour plowing, terracing, and shelterbelts. By 1938 soil loss in demonstration counties had fallen by 65 percent.

lo.label: A
lo.text: TEXT 1 · Oral history, recorded 1978. "April 14, 1935. We called it Black Sunday after. The morning was clear and warm and people hung wash out."

lo.label: B
lo.text: "The cloud came from the north and it was not a rain cloud. It was two thousand feet high and brown. My mother put wet sheets over the windows and it still came in."

lo.label: C
lo.text: "We had six good years on that land before that. People say the farmers should have known. Nobody told us. The government men came and taught contour plowing in 1937, two years after."

lo.label: D
lo.text: TEXT 2 · From an agricultural history. The southern Plains were grassland whose deep roots held the soil through droughts that came about every twenty years.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Between 1925 and 1930, tractors broke about 5 million acres of that sod for wheat. Wheat roots are shallow. When the drought came in 1931, nothing held the soil.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Federal soil programs began in 1935 and taught contour plowing and shelterbelts. By 1938 soil loss in those counties had dropped by 65 percent.

qs.q: Use the timeline to explain why the good years came before the disaster.
qs.a: The sod broken between 1925 and 1930 grew wheat well while the rain held, which is the six good years the speaker remembers. The drought returned on its usual cycle in 1931, and because wheat roots are shallow there was nothing left holding the soil.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. blame) and paragraph E (i.e. plowing).
Integrate both texts to explain what caused the Dust Bowl.
qs.a: Deep-rooted grassland had carried the southern Plains through droughts recurring every twenty years or so. Tractors broke about 5 million acres of that sod for shallow-rooted wheat between 1925 and 1930, which produced the six good years the speaker recalls. When drought returned in 1931 nothing held the soil, and by Black Sunday in 1935 a brown cloud two thousand feet high crossed the region. Conservation programs begun that year cut soil loss 65 percent by 1938.

qs.q:
sod: Sod is the top layer of soil held together by grass roots.
contour plowing: Contour plowing means plowing across a slope instead of up and down it, so water and soil stay put.
Describe the connection between shallow wheat roots and soil blowing away.
qs.a: Because wheat roots are shallow and die back each year, they could not grip the soil the way grass roots had, so when drought dried the surface there was nothing to hold it and the wind lifted it.

hi.label: A
hi.text: TEXT 1 · From a science magazine. Sleep is when the brain files what it learned. During deep sleep, patterns of activity recorded in the hippocampus during the day are replayed, faster, and copied into longer-term storage in the cortex.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Experiments show the effect plainly. Students taught a list of word pairs and then allowed to sleep recall about 40 percent more than students taught at the same hour and kept awake the same length of time.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The same holds for physical skills. Typing a new finger sequence improves overnight without further practice, and the improvement shows up in sleep, not in the hours of wakefulness before it.

hi.label: D
hi.text: TEXT 2 · From a sleep laboratory’s guidance for schools. The replay finding is robust, and it is often used to argue that students should simply sleep more. The harder part is that not all sleep does this work equally.

hi.label: E
hi.text: Deep sleep is concentrated in the first half of the night; the REM sleep tied to skill and emotional memory clusters in the last two hours before waking. A student who sleeps seven hours instead of nine does not lose a slice of each. She loses most of her REM.

hi.label: F
hi.text: This is why a shortened night hurts skill learning more than fact learning, and why sleeping in on weekends does not repay the debt evenly.

lo.label: A
lo.text: TEXT 1 · From a science magazine. Sleep is when the brain files what it learned. In deep sleep, patterns recorded during the day are replayed faster and copied into longer-term storage.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Experiments show it clearly. Students taught word pairs and then allowed to sleep recall about 40 percent more than students kept awake for the same time.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The same holds for skills. Typing a new finger pattern improves overnight without more practice, and the gain shows up during sleep.

lo.label: D
lo.text: TEXT 2 · From a sleep lab’s guidance for schools. The replay finding is solid, and it is used to argue that students should sleep more. The harder part is that not all sleep does this work equally.

lo.label: E
lo.text: Deep sleep comes in the first half of the night. The REM sleep tied to skills comes in the last two hours before waking. A student who sleeps seven hours instead of nine loses most of her REM, not a slice of each.

lo.label: F
lo.text: That is why a short night hurts skill learning more than fact learning.

qs.q: Use the diagram to explain why a short night hurts skill learning most.
qs.a: Deep sleep, which handles facts, falls in the first four hours and survives a short night. REM, which handles skills, is concentrated in hours eight and nine, so cutting two hours off the end removes most of the REM and leaves the fact-storing sleep nearly untouched.

qs.q: Paragraph B (i.e. evidence) and paragraph E (i.e. timing).
Integrate both texts into advice you could give a student.
qs.a: Sleep replays the day’s patterns and copies them into long-term storage, which is why sleeping students recall about 40 percent more word pairs and why a typing sequence improves overnight. But the two kinds of sleep are not spread evenly: deep sleep runs early and REM runs in the last two hours. Cutting a night short removes mostly REM, so a student practicing a skill loses more than one studying facts.

qs.q:
hippocampus: The hippocampus is the part of the brain that records new experiences before they are stored long term.
robust: A robust finding is one that holds up when the experiment is repeated.
Describe the connection between sleeping and getting better at a skill without practicing.
qs.a: Because the brain replays the finger sequence during sleep rather than during waking hours, the movement is rehearsed internally overnight, so performance improves by morning even though no additional practice took place.

hi.label: A
hi.text: On a Norwegian island 800 miles from the North Pole, a concrete entrance juts out of a mountainside. Behind it, a tunnel runs 400 feet into permafrost.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds backup copies of crop seeds from almost every country. More than a million samples are stored there, each sealed in a foil packet inside a labeled box.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The vault does not own the seeds. Each depositing country keeps ownership and can withdraw its own boxes at any time, the way a bank holds a safe-deposit box it cannot open.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The site was chosen for its cold. Even if the refrigeration fails, the surrounding permafrost keeps the chambers below freezing without power.

hi.label: E

hi.label: F
hi.text: That sequence is the vault working exactly as designed. It is not a museum. It is a spare copy.

lo.label: A
lo.text: On a Norwegian island 800 miles from the North Pole, a concrete entrance sticks out of a mountainside. Behind it a tunnel runs 400 feet into frozen ground.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds backup copies of crop seeds from almost every country. More than a million samples are stored there in sealed foil packets.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The vault does not own the seeds. Each country keeps its own boxes and can take them back, like a bank holding a box it cannot open.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The site was chosen for its cold. If the freezers fail, the frozen ground keeps the rooms below freezing without power.

lo.label: E
lo.text: There has been one withdrawal. In 2015 researchers in Syria, cut off from their own seed bank by war, asked for their deposits back. They grew the seeds, harvested new ones, and sent fresh samples back.

lo.label: F
lo.text: That is the vault working as designed. It is not a museum. It is a spare copy.

qs.q: Use the diagram to explain why the vault was built inside a frozen mountain.
qs.a: The rock puts 400 feet between the seeds and any storm, flood, or conflict outside, and the surrounding permafrost keeps the chambers below freezing even if the refrigeration loses power.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. ownership) and paragraph E (i.e. withdrawal).
Summarize what the vault is for and how the Syrian withdrawal showed it working.
qs.a: The vault stores backup copies of more than a million crop seed samples from nearly every country, each still owned by its depositor. When war cut Syrian researchers off from their own gene bank in 2015, they withdrew their deposits, grew the seeds elsewhere, and returned fresh samples, which is the cycle the vault was designed for.

qs.q:
permafrost: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year, even in summer.
deposits: Deposits are things placed somewhere for safekeeping, to be taken back later.
Describe the connection between the location and what happens if the power fails.
qs.a: Because the chambers are surrounded by ground that never thaws, a power failure does not warm them, so the seeds stay frozen while repairs are made.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A crowd of 70,000 people can be measured. At Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, the noise has reached 142 decibels, louder than a jet engine at close range.

hi.label: B
hi.text: Decibels do not work the way most numbers do. The scale is logarithmic: every increase of 10 means the sound is ten times more intense. A 120-decibel crowd is not slightly louder than a 110-decibel crowd. It is ten times as intense.

hi.label: C
hi.text: The shape of the building matters more than the size of the crowd. A bowl with a low roof traps sound and reflects it back down onto the field. An open stadium of the same capacity measures far quieter.

hi.label: D
hi.text: Teams have learned to use it. A visiting quarterback cannot be heard calling plays, so the offense must use silent signals, and false-start penalties rise.

hi.label: E
hi.text: There is a cost. Sustained exposure above 100 decibels damages hearing, and stadium workers are exposed for whole seasons rather than single afternoons.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Some clubs now issue earplugs to staff. Almost none issue them to fans, who generally decline.

lo.label: A
lo.text: A crowd of 70,000 people can be measured. At one stadium in Kansas City, the noise has reached 142 decibels, louder than a jet engine up close.

lo.label: B
lo.text: Decibels do not work like most numbers. Every increase of 10 means the sound is ten times more intense. A 120-decibel crowd is ten times as intense as a 110-decibel crowd.

lo.label: C
lo.text: The shape of the building matters more than the size of the crowd. A bowl with a low roof traps sound and sends it back down. An open stadium the same size is much quieter.

lo.label: D
lo.text: Teams use it. A visiting quarterback cannot be heard calling plays, so the offense uses silent signals and makes more mistakes.

lo.label: E
lo.text: There is a cost. Long exposure above 100 decibels damages hearing, and workers are there all season.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Some clubs give earplugs to staff. Almost none give them to fans.

qs.q: Use the chart to explain why 142 decibels is far worse than it sounds.
qs.a: The scale multiplies rather than adds. Every 10 decibels is ten times the intensity, so the gap from 100 to 142 is not a small step past the damage threshold but thousands of times more intense sound.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. architecture) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Summarize why some stadiums are louder than others and what that costs.
qs.a: Crowd size matters less than shape: a low-roofed bowl reflects sound back onto the field while an open stadium of the same capacity is far quieter. The noise helps the home team, because visiting offenses cannot hear play calls and make more errors. It also damages the hearing of workers exposed to it all season.

qs.q:
logarithmic: A logarithmic scale multiplies at each step instead of adding the same amount.
sustained: Sustained means kept up over a long period rather than happening once.
Describe the connection between a stadium’s roof and how loud it is.
qs.a: Because a low roof stops sound from escaping upward, the noise reflects back down onto the field and adds to what the crowd is producing, so the same number of people sound far louder than in an open stadium.

hi.label: A
hi.text: In 1930s Britain, a stockbroker named Nicholas Winton planned a skiing holiday. A friend asked him instead to come to Prague and see what was happening to refugee families there.

hi.label: B
hi.text: He went. Czechoslovakia had already lost its border regions to Germany, and thousands of families had fled inland with nowhere to go and no country willing to take them.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Britain would admit children under seventeen, but only with a sponsor, a foster family, and a £50 guarantee for each child. Winton set up an office in a hotel and began collecting names.

hi.label: D
hi.text: He sent lists to newspapers, forged entry documents when the paperwork ran behind, and arranged eight trains. Six hundred sixty-nine children reached London.

hi.label: E
hi.text: A ninth train, carrying 250 children, was scheduled for September 1, 1939. Germany invaded Poland that morning and the borders closed. That train never left.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Winton told almost no one. His wife found the scrapbook of names in the attic in 1988, nearly fifty years later.

lo.text: In 1930s Britain, a stockbroker named Nicholas Winton planned a skiing holiday. A friend asked him instead to come to Prague and see what was happening to refugee families.

lo.label: B
lo.text: He went. Czechoslovakia had lost its border lands to Germany, and thousands of families had fled inland with nowhere to go.

lo.label: C

lo.label: E
lo.text: A ninth train, carrying 250 children, was set for September 1, 1939. Germany invaded Poland that morning and the borders closed. That train never left.

lo.label: F

qs.q: Use the timeline to explain why Winton could not simply move all the children at once.
qs.a: Britain required a sponsor, a foster family, and a £50 guarantee for every single child, so each name on his list needed months of separate arrangements before that child could board a train.

qs.q: Paragraph D (i.e. organizing) and paragraph E (i.e. the closing).
Summarize what Winton did and what stopped him.
qs.a: Winton went to Prague in 1938, opened an office in a hotel, and matched refugee children one at a time to the sponsors, foster families, and £50 guarantees Britain demanded. Eight trains carried 669 children to London. A ninth carrying 250 was due to leave on September 1, 1939, the morning Germany invaded Poland and the borders closed.

qs.q:
refugee: A refugee is someone forced to leave home to escape war or danger.
guarantee: A guarantee is a promise, often backed by money, that something will be covered.
Describe the connection between the invasion of Poland and the ninth train.
qs.a: Because the invasion that morning closed the borders the train had to cross, the 250 children who were already scheduled and approved could not leave, and the rescue ended where it stood.

hi.label: A
hi.text: Cut a tree across and you get a record. Each pale band and dark band together make one year of growth.

hi.label: B
hi.text: The width of a ring is a weather report. A wet year with good light produces a wide ring. A drought year produces a narrow one. A tree that lived 400 years carries 400 measurements.

hi.label: C
hi.text: Because every tree in a region shares the same weather, their patterns match. Scientists overlap the ring patterns of living trees with those in old beams and buried logs, extending the record back thousands of years.

hi.label: D
hi.text: That overlapping makes tree rings a calendar. A beam in a cliff dwelling can be dated to the exact year it was cut, not a century or a range.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The rings recorded something else in the American Southwest: a drought lasting from 1276 to 1299. Within that window, the large cliff settlements were abandoned.

hi.label: F
hi.text: The rings do not say the drought caused people to leave. They establish that the two happened at the same time, which is the kind of fact an argument has to start from.

lo.label: A
lo.text: Cut a tree across and you get a record. Each pale band and dark band together make one year of growth.

lo.label: B
lo.text: The width of a ring is a weather report. A wet year makes a wide ring. A dry year makes a narrow one. A tree that lived 400 years carries 400 measurements.

lo.label: C
lo.text: Every tree in an area shares the same weather, so their patterns match. Scientists overlap patterns from living trees, old beams, and buried logs to reach back thousands of years.

lo.label: D
lo.text: That overlap makes tree rings a calendar. A beam in a cliff dwelling can be dated to the exact year it was cut.

lo.label: E
lo.text: The rings recorded something else in the Southwest: a drought from 1276 to 1299. In those years the large cliff settlements were abandoned.

lo.label: F
lo.text: The rings do not say the drought made people leave. They show the two happened at the same time.

qs.q: Use the diagram to explain how rings from a living tree help date a wooden beam.
qs.a: Trees in one region share weather, so their ring patterns match. A scientist finds where the pattern in the beam lines up with the pattern in a living tree, which fixes the beam’s rings to known years and gives the exact year it was cut.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. overlapping) and paragraph F (i.e. caution).
Summarize what tree rings can and cannot tell us.
qs.a: Each ring records one year, and its width records whether that year was wet or dry, so a single tree holds centuries of weather. Overlapping patterns from living trees, beams, and buried logs turn that into a calendar accurate to the year, which showed a drought from 1276 to 1299 in the Southwest. The rings date that drought alongside the abandonment of the cliff settlements but do not prove it caused them.

qs.q:
drought: A drought is a long stretch of time with far less rain than usual.
abandoned: Abandoned means left behind and no longer lived in or used.
Describe the connection between two events happening at the same time and one causing the other.
qs.a: Because the rings only show that the drought and the abandonment fall in the same years, they establish timing rather than cause, and an argument about why people left has to add other evidence.

g4-49.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a 400-year tree carries 400 measurements" or "a beam can be dated to the exact year." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

hi.label: A
hi.text: A survey ship looking for a wreck does not look. It listens.

hi.label: B
hi.text: A sonar unit towed behind the ship sends out a pulse of sound and measures how long the echo takes to return. Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so the delay converts directly into depth.

hi.label: C
hi.text: One pulse gives one depth. A modern multibeam unit fans out hundreds of beams at once, sweeping a strip of sea floor as wide as the water is deep.

hi.label: D
hi.text: The ship then drives back and forth in overlapping lanes, the way a mower crosses a lawn. A search area of a few hundred square miles can take weeks.

hi.label: E
hi.text: The result is not a photograph. It is a grid of depths, colored by height, in which a wreck appears as a shape a few meters proud of a flat plain.

hi.label: F
hi.text: Most of what the sweep finds is not the target. Analysts sort through boulders, rock ridges, and containers lost off cargo ships before anything worth a second pass turns up.

lo.label: A
lo.text: A survey ship looking for a wreck does not look. It listens.

lo.label: B
lo.text: A sonar unit towed behind the ship sends out a pulse of sound and times the echo. Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so the delay gives the depth.

lo.label: C
lo.text: One pulse gives one depth. A modern multibeam unit sends hundreds of beams at once, sweeping a strip of sea floor as wide as the water is deep.

lo.label: D
lo.text: The ship drives back and forth in overlapping lanes, like mowing a lawn. A few hundred square miles can take weeks.

lo.label: E
lo.text: The result is not a photo. It is a grid of depths, colored by height, where a wreck shows up as a shape a few meters above a flat plain.

lo.label: F
lo.text: Most of what the sweep finds is not the target. Analysts sort through boulders, rock ridges, and lost shipping containers first.

qs.q: Use the diagram to explain why the travel time is divided in half.
qs.a: The sound has to travel down to the sea floor and back up to the ship, so the measured time covers the distance twice. Halving it gives the one-way depth.

qs.q: Paragraph C (i.e. sweeping) and paragraph F (i.e. sorting).
Summarize how a survey ship finds a wreck.
qs.a: Sonar sends pulses of sound to the bottom and times the echoes, converting the delay into depth at about 1,500 meters per second. A multibeam unit does this with hundreds of beams at once, covering a strip as wide as the water is deep, and the ship runs overlapping lanes until the area is mapped. The result is a colored depth grid in which analysts look for a shape standing a few meters above the flat sea floor.

qs.q:
sonar: Sonar finds objects underwater by sending out sound and timing the echo.
analysts: Analysts are people whose job is to study data carefully and decide what it shows.
Describe the connection between the width of one sweep and how long a search takes.
qs.a: Because each pass only covers a strip as wide as the water is deep, a shallow area needs far more lanes to cover the same ground, so the number of passes rather than the size of the ship sets how many weeks the search will run.
